If there's nothing on your laptop that you need to back up you might be better off just reformatting everything and starting over.

I recommend installing Windows first. Use the windows partition manager during the install process to create a partition for Windows to live on. I think Windows needs a minimum of 20G to install to. You'll probably need a little more than that for whatever else you'll be installing. Leave the rest of the drive un-formatted. Once Windows has finished installing you can install whatever version of Linux you want.

When it gets time to select the partition to install to, some versions of Linux will have an option to automatically install along side Windows while others will require you to manually create partitions. Just pick whatever you're comfortable with. If you're going to create your own partitions, you will need a minimum of the root ("/") partition and a swap partition. If you want to get tricky (for advanced users) you can do things like shared swap, home, and boot partitions between multiple installed distros, but that can be confusing if you don't know what you're doing.

If your Linux distro has been installed correctly, when you reboot GRUB will ask you which OS you want to boot to. it should show options for Windows and whatever Linux distro(s) you've installed. Select whatever one you want, press enter, and you should be all set with your new multi-boot system.

A couple of notes:

  • During the Linux install you will be asked where to install GRUB. Select the root of the drive. e.g. if your primary boot drive is /dev/sda you want to install GRUB to /dev/sda (NOT /dev/sda1, /dev/sda2, etc...).

  • You are now using the GRUB boot loader to boot to your OS. This is the first thing that your computer loads and you cannot boot to any OS without it. Sometimes Windows will overwrite GRUB (e.g. running a Windows repair operation), or you might delete your Linux partition to install a different distro. If your boot process changes, doesn't work, or doesn't seem right, you don't have to start from scratch. you just need to re-install grub. You can do this by booting to a live CD and running "grub-install" with the correct options.

  • Bootable Live USB drives can be a lifesaver. If you want to pull data from your hard drive, most live distros will be able to at least read Windows partitions. Once you're done backing things up, you can install directly from the live USB. UNetbootin works on Windows, Linux, and MAC.
